client:
Lately, I've just been feeling so empty since my dog passed away last month. Everything reminds me of him—his favorite spots around the house, our walking routes, even simple things like hearing his collar jingle when he'd shake. I used to love our daily walks, but now I can barely bring myself to go outside because it just hurts too much.

I'm not really sure how talking about this will help. He's gone, and no amount of talking will change that. Part of me thinks I should just try to push through it, but another part feels like that's betraying his memory somehow.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying such deep grief and love for your dog—those memories feel both precious and painful right now. When you say "no amount of talking will change" his absence, I hear how final that loss feels, yet part of you is still here, reaching out. Would it feel okay to explore what honoring his memory might look like for you in this moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Honoring his memory sounds nice in theory, but I don’t even know where to start. It feels like anything I do will just remind me of what I’ve lost. I tried looking at photos of him the other day, and I ended up crying for hours. It’s like every time I try to connect with those memories, I just feel worse. Maybe it’s better to just avoid it altogether for now.
therapist: I hear how overwhelming these moments of remembrance feel—like the love and the loss are crashing together in a way that's too much to hold right now. When you tried looking at photos, that pain felt raw and immediate, didn't it? Could we sit with what makes the idea of honoring him feel both important and frightening right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It feels important because he meant so much to me—he was my companion, my comfort, and honestly, my best friend. But it’s frightening because it feels like I’m opening a door to all this pain again. What if I can’t handle it? What if I just end up feeling worse, like I did with the photos? I don’t know if I’m strong enough to face that right now.
therapist: It sounds like honoring him is deeply tied to both the love you shared and the pain of his absence—two feelings that are so intertwined. When you talk about opening that door, it seems like you’re worried about being overwhelmed by the grief, even as you want to hold onto the connection. Would it feel possible to take small steps, like choosing just one photo or memory to sit with for a moment, and see how that feels?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess I could try looking at just one photo, but even that feels scary. What if I start crying and can’t stop? Or what if it doesn’t feel like enough, and I end up feeling guilty for not doing more? It’s like I’m stuck between wanting to honor him and being terrified of the emotions that might come up. I don’t know if I’m ready for that yet.
therapist: Your voice softened just now as you described this fear—like the thought of facing even one photo carries so much weight. It makes sense that you'd feel torn between wanting to honor him and protecting yourself from that wave of emotion. Would it feel safer to start with something gentler, like remembering his favorite treat or the sound of his footsteps, rather than diving straight into photos?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That... that actually sounds a little easier. I could try thinking about how he used to get so excited for peanut butter treats—his little tail would wag like crazy. But even that makes my chest feel tight. What if focusing on happy memories just makes the sadness worse because I can’t have those moments anymore? It still feels like I’m losing him all over again.
therapist: There's something so tender in how you describe his excitement—that love is still so alive even through the tightness in your chest. It makes sense that joy and sadness would swirl together when remembering those moments. What if we just stayed with that peanut butter memory for a moment, noticing how it feels without needing to push away either the warmth or the ache?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: It’s hard to stay with that memory because it feels like I’m teetering on the edge of something—like if I let myself feel the warmth, the sadness might swallow me whole. I want to hold onto those happy moments, but it’s so painful knowing I’ll never see him wag his tail like that again. Maybe I’m not ready to face both at the same time.
therapist: I hear how delicate this feels—like holding a fragile balance between joy and sorrow, where leaning too far either way might feel unbearable. That fear of being swallowed by sadness makes so much sense when the love was this deep. Would it feel okay to take a breath with that memory, letting it be as big or as small as you need in this moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Taking a breath with that memory feels... I don’t know, a little easier, but also strange. It’s like I’m holding onto something fragile, like you said. Part of me wants to stay there, but another part is scared of how much it hurts. Maybe I can try that, but I’m still not sure if I’m ready to let myself feel all of it yet.
therapist: It sounds like you're finding a small space to hold that memory—one that feels a little safer, even if it’s still tender. It’s okay to take it at your own pace, letting yourself feel what you can when you’re ready. Would it feel helpful to pause here for a moment and notice how it feels to have taken this small step?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Pausing feels... a little grounding, but also kind of strange. I’m not used to sitting with these feelings—usually, I just try to push them away or distract myself. It’s like I’m afraid if I let myself feel even a little bit, it’ll all come rushing in, and I won’t be able to handle it. I guess I’m still not sure if this is the right way to honor him or if I’m just making things harder for myself.
therapist: I hear that uncertainty—like you're testing the waters of something new, where even small pauses feel both grounding and unfamiliar. It makes sense that letting yourself feel even a little might bring up worries about being overwhelmed. What’s coming up for you as you notice that tension between wanting to honor him and fearing the rush of emotions?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: It’s like I’m stuck in this loop where I want to honor him because he deserves that, but every time I try, I feel like I’m drowning in sadness. I guess part of me worries that if I let myself feel it fully, I’ll never be able to pull myself back out. I don’t know if I’m strong enough to handle that kind of pain, even though I know he meant so much to me.
therapist: It sounds like honoring him feels like stepping into an ocean of grief—where the love you have for him pulls you toward the memories, but the fear of drowning in sadness holds you back. That worry about being overwhelmed makes so much sense when the loss feels this big. Would it feel okay to explore what “pulling yourself back out” might look like, even in small ways?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I’ve never really thought about how to “pull myself back out” because I’ve always just avoided the feelings altogether. Maybe it’s something like taking a deep breath or stepping away for a moment, but even that feels uncertain. What if I try to pull back and it doesn’t work? What if I’m stuck in that sadness forever? I don’t know if I trust myself to navigate that yet.
therapist: Your voice quickened just now as you shared this uncertainty—like the idea of trusting yourself to navigate these feelings feels daunting and unfamiliar. It’s okay to feel unsure about how to pull back; this is new territory, and it’s natural to feel hesitant. What would it feel like to experiment with small steps, like taking that deep breath or pausing, and noticing how it feels in the moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
